critic_changes: Tension: the claim that income per person only clearly passed its 1994 level (2,570) in 2025 is wrong. The data show 2,585 in 2017 and 2,573 in 2019, both above 1994. Rewrote it to compare 2024 (2,567) with the 2017 level (2,585), which 2025 (2,665) was the first year to pass. Also changed 'among the best years in the Pacific' to the press release's wording ('one of the strongest performances in the Pacific').

Arc: removed 'as the gas project's construction ended' from the 2017–2025 era. The IMF ties the project's completion to the 2015–16 slowdown, which falls in the 2006–2016 era, not to the years since 2017.

Arc: changed 'A rebound since 2022, helped by the reopened Porgera gold mine' so that Porgera and easier access to foreign exchange are tied to 2025, as the sources do, not to the whole period since 2022. Growth was 1.9 percent in 2023.

Thread 'New mines, then a crisis': added an ADB citation for the severe drought in 1997, which the two existing quotes did not cover. Checked the 1992 quote against the PDF and it is verbatim; the two-column layout only made it look split.

Changed the text from 'building work ended' to 'the project was completed' to match.

growth_story.headline: Mines and gas have lifted Papua New Guinea's output in bursts, but income per person grew only 0.7 percent a year over the last decade.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990 Papua New Guinea's income per person has moved in four eras, each tied to its mines, oil and gas. In 1990–1997 it grew 2.1 percent a year: new gold mines and oil fields lifted growth to 9.9 percent in 1992 and 14.0 in 1993, before heavy borrowing ran down foreign exchange reserves and a severe drought hit in 1997. In 1998–2005 it fell 2.5 percent a year as drought, the Asian financial crisis, loose control of spending and low commodity prices took hold, and income per person dropped from 2,311 dollars in 1997 to 1,822 in 2004. In 2006–2016 higher commodity prices and the PNG LNG gas project, which came on stream in 2014, lifted growth to 2.9 percent a year, with a jump of 10.6 percent in 2014. Since 2017 growth has averaged 0.5 percent a year, as low commodity prices, droughts, earthquakes, COVID-19 and long shortages of foreign exchange hit, with a fall of 5.2 percent in 2020. Growth picked up from 2022 and reached 3.8 percent in 2025, helped by more output from the reopened Porgera gold mine and easier access to foreign exchange, which took income per person to its highest level yet.

threads.title: New mines, then a crisis
threads.text: New gold mines and oil fields opened in mid-1992, and income per person grew 9.9 percent in 1992 and 14.0 in 1993. Spending financed by heavy domestic borrowing then ran down foreign exchange reserves after oil prices fell in 1994, and a severe drought followed in 1997, when income per person fell 7.3 percent.

threads.title: The gas project boom
threads.text: Higher commodity prices from the mid-2000s and the PNG LNG gas project lifted growth to 2.9 percent a year in 2006–2016, with a 10.6 percent jump in 2014 when the project began operating. Once the project was completed and export prices fell, growth slowed in 2015–16 and the economy leaned more on gas and mining exports.

threads.title: Shocks and scarce foreign exchange
threads.text: Over the last decade low commodity prices, droughts, earthquakes and COVID-19 have hit growth, and income per person fell 2.6 percent in 2018 and 5.2 percent in 2020. Firms and households could not get enough foreign exchange for years, which held back private investment and spending; exchange rate and market reforms have since eased the shortages.

threads.title: Growth with few jobs
threads.text: Mining and gas earn most export income but employ few people, and formal jobs have not kept pace with a fast-growing working-age population. Most people still live from informal work and subsistence farming, so strong output growth has done less for living standards.

since_last_year.text: In 2025 income per person grew 3.8 percent, the fastest since 2015. The World Bank credits more output from the reopened Porgera gold mine and easier access to foreign exchange after exchange rate and market reforms. In October 2026 it expected growth to slow in 2026 as the Porgera boost fades and El Niño weighs on activity.

citations.title: Papua New Guinea, Macro Poverty Outlook, October 2026
citations.quote: In 2026, growth is estimated to slow to 3.5 percent as Porgera’s boost fades and El Niño weighs on activity.

citations.title: Papua New Guinea's Economy Grows, but Jobs Gap Remains
citations.quote: This was supported by strong gold and LNG production, alongside exchange rate reforms, which improved the business environment beyond the resource sector.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe strong, resource-driven growth, with 2025 one of the strongest years in the Pacific. Yet income per person in 2024, at 2,567 dollars, was still below its 2017 level of 2,585, and only in 2025, at 2,665, did it pass it. The World Bank notes that this growth creates few jobs while the working-age population grows fast.
